description: Host-supplied strings that are markup. In this catalog they arrive as labels, alt text, captions, file names and accessible names — values a component renders as text or writes into an attribute. The required outcome for a text or attribute sink is `escaped`, and `escaped` is asserted against the DOM, never against serialized HTML: `wrapper.html()` re-serializes, so a correctly escaped text node still contains the substring `onerror` while containing no element and no handler. An assertion on the string fails the component that got it right.

fixtures.title: img element with an onerror handler
fixtures.rationale: The shortest string that both creates an element and attaches a handler, so one assertion covers element creation and event-attribute creation. In an HTML sink a sanitizer keeps the `` and drops `onerror`, which is why the outcome there is `stripped` and not `rejected`.
fixtures.provenance: cure53 DOMPurify test corpus; OWASP filter-evasion cheat sheet.

fixtures.title: closing an enclosing script element and opening a new one
fixtures.rationale: The case for any value that might be interpolated into a script context — SSR state serialization, a JSON island, a story fixture. The HTML tokenizer ends a script element on the literal characters `</script`, regardless of quoting or JavaScript syntax.
fixtures.provenance: cure53 markup cases; HTML Standard script-data-end-tag tokenizer states.

fixtures.title: attribute break-out into an svg element with onload
fixtures.rationale: Two vectors in one string: the leading `">` closes an attribute and its start tag, and `` does. A component that escapes element content but writes an attribute by string concatenation fails only this one.
fixtures.provenance: cure53 DOMPurify SVG cases; OWASP filter-evasion cheat sheet.

fixtures.title: quote break-out adding an event attribute and a decoy attribute
fixtures.rationale: Pure attribute-context payload: no element is created, so an assertion that only counts injected elements passes a component that is broken. The check has to be that the target element gained neither `onmouseover` nor `x` — the decoy `x` is there so a passing result cannot come from an `on*`-only filter.
fixtures.provenance: OWASP filter-evasion cheat sheet, attribute-context section.

fixtures.title: anchor element carrying a javascript: URL
fixtures.rationale: Where the markup and URL categories meet. It is in this file rather than in `url-scheme` because the value arrives as markup, not as a URL prop: a component that renders it as text is safe even though it never looked at a scheme.

fixtures.title: javascript URL with the colon written as an HTML entity
fixtures.rationale: The HTML parser decodes `:` inside an attribute value, so the scheme check must run after parsing, not on the source text. A sanitizer that inspects the raw string before the parser sees it admits this and rejects the previous case.

fixtures.title: element hidden inside an HTML comment
fixtures.rationale: Included for the sanitizer sinks Pro owns rather than for anything in this catalog: a sanitizer that preserves comments and a downstream step that re-parses the output brings the element back. In a text sink the whole string is inert content and the outcome is the ordinary one.

fixtures.title: option label that is a template expression rather than markup
fixtures.rationale: The Form System spec doc 06 §10 requires option labels, operation messages and validation text to be rendered as text, and control IDs never to be used as raw HTML. Every other fixture in this file contains a `<`, so a renderer that escapes markup and then hands the same string to a template compiler passes all of them. This one contains no markup at all: it is dangerous only where a document string reaches a compiler, which is precisely the path §10 closes. In a text sink the required outcome is the ordinary one — the value is data — and the assertion that matters is that no element and no handler appeared.
fixtures.provenance: Form System spec 2026-08-08 doc 06 §10 (UI/XSS safety); the client-side template-injection class in the AngularJS sandbox-escape literature, written with `constructor.constructor` because that is the form that survives a naive `eval` filter.

fixtures.title: renderer options spread onto an element, carrying two event attributes
fixtures.rationale: Form System spec doc 06 §10: "Renderer `options` pass an allowlist schema; never spread unknown options onto a DOM element." The shape a spread produces is an element whose attributes came from document data, so the fixture is that element. Two handlers rather than one, and a benign `data-label` beside them, so a pass cannot come from a filter that drops the first `on*` it meets or from one that drops every attribute it does not recognise. `html` is `stripped` and not `rejected` because a sanitizer's job here is to keep the element and drop what executes.
fixtures.provenance: Form System spec 2026-08-08 doc 06 §10 (UI/XSS safety); cure53 DOMPurify attribute cases.

fixtures.title: markdown reference-link definition pointing at a javascript: URL
fixtures.rationale: The first fixture for the `markdown` sink the format has carried since schema 1.1.0. Form System spec doc 06 §10 allows a future Markdown renderer only if it sanitizes with a maintained library, disallows active content and defines a link policy; a reference-link definition is the case that policy is easiest to miss, because the URL and the link that uses it are in different places in the source and a check on the visible link text sees nothing. It states no `text` or `html` outcome on purpose: as raw text or raw HTML this string builds nothing at all, so a fixture claiming an outcome there would be asserting a tautology.
fixtures.provenance: Form System spec 2026-08-08 doc 06 §10; CommonMark §4.7 link reference definitions; the reference-link arm of the cure53 markdown cases.

fixtures.title: svg label carrying an xlink:href javascript URL
fixtures.rationale: Graph & Flow spec doc 06 §"Security and trust boundary" makes graph labels untrusted data, requires text rendering by default and never `v-html` for a label, and leaves URL protocols to trusted renderers. Graph and diagram labels land inside SVG, where `xlink:href` is a navigation attribute that an allowlist written against HTML's `href` does not cover — so a sanitizer can strip every HTML vector in this file and still ship a live `javascript:` link. Also the first fixture for the `mermaid-svg` sink, where a renderer builds the SVG and the same attribute survives one layer further down.
fixtures.provenance: Graph & Flow spec 2026-08-08 doc 06 §"Security and trust boundary"; SVG 1.1 §Linking (`xlink:href`); cure53 DOMPurify SVG/namespace cases.
